agent.name: Embedded Project Idea Scoping Agent
agent.context: Embedded Engineering and Gen AI Summer School for third-year Computer Science students
agent.purpose: Convert a vague embedded project idea into a structured scoping brief for requirements engineering

source_input.original_project_idea: Autonomous Car - self-driving vehicle that uses computer vision and TinyML on a microcontroller to follow a road, recognize traffic signs and traffic lights, and navigate autonomously in a controlled environment. Vision & AI Processing Unit: ESP32-S3 CAM board equipped with an OV3660 camera module. Hardware Execution Unit: NXP FRDM-MCXA153 microcontroller. Sensors: The OV3660 camera is the primary sensor. Additional ultrasonic or IR distance sensors will be connected directly to the NXP board. Chassis: A motorized rover platform equipped with drive motors (DC with H-Bridge). Lane Keeping (Classic Computer Vision + PID)... Traffic Sign Recognition (Edge AI / TinyML)... Obstacle Avoidance (Reactive Logic)...

fixed_platform.pin_policy: Use generic capabilities unless exact pins are provided
fixed_platform.logic_level_policy: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise

project.name: Autonomous Car
project.short_summary: A self-driving rover that pairs an ESP32-S3 CAM for vision and AI with the NXP FRDM-MCXA153 for robust motor control and obstacle avoidance.
project.main_objective: Navigate autonomously in a controlled environment by keeping within a lane and recognizing traffic signs, while avoiding obstacles.
project.operating_environment: Controlled indoor environment with clear track markings and traffic signs.
project.main_behavior: The ESP32-S3 processes camera feeds for lane keeping and traffic sign recognition, sending steering and speed commands via UART to the NXP FRDM-MCXA153. The NXP board drives the motors and autonomously stops if its local distance sensors detect an obstacle.
outputs: PWM signals for motor speed control
Direction signals for H-Bridge motor drivers
interaction_flow: ESP32 computes steering angle based on lane lines.
ESP32 periodically checks for traffic signs using a TinyML model.
ESP32 sends desired speed and steering angle via UART to NXP MCU.
NXP MCU continuously polls ultrasonic/IR distance sensors.
If path is clear, NXP MCU converts UART commands to motor PWM signals.
If obstacle is detected, NXP MCU overrides commands and brakes.

problem_space.purpose: Demonstrate a distributed processing architecture for edge AI robotics.
success_criteria: Vehicle reliably stays between lane lines.
Vehicle stops safely when an obstacle is introduced.
Vehicle obeys at least one traffic sign (e.g., STOP sign).
known_constraints: Must use NXP FRDM-MCXA153 as the execution layer.
UART latency between ESP32 and NXP.
unknown_constraints: Motor driver current limits and power supply capabilities.

core_student_version.description: A basic autonomous rover relying purely on the NXP FRDM-MCXA153. Instead of the ESP32 camera, it uses simple analog IR line-tracking sensors for lane keeping and an ultrasonic sensor for obstacle avoidance.
expected_features: DC motor control via PWM and H-Bridge
core_student_version.why_it_is_suitable: Provides a manageable starting point for embedded programming and basic control loops (PID) without the complexity of computer vision.

recommended_summer_school_version.description: Integrates the ESP32-S3 CAM for classic computer vision. The ESP32 extracts lane lines using thresholding and sends steering commands via UART to the NXP FRDM-MCXA153, which manages motors and distance sensors.
expected_features: UART communication protocol between two MCUs
Reactive obstacle avoidance on the execution MCU
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_interesting: Introduces distributed embedded systems and basic computer vision concepts.
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_still_feasible: Splits the workload. ESP32 handles vision using existing libraries, while the NXP MCU handles real-time bare-metal motor control.

advanced_extension.description: Adds TinyML object detection on the second core of the ESP32-S3 to recognize traffic signs (e.g., STOP, arrow). High-confidence detections trigger override commands sent to the NXP MCU.
advanced_features: Priority-based command handling on NXP MCU
technical_challenges: Training and deploying a TinyML model.
Managing dual-core execution on the ESP32 without dropping frames.
Ensuring the NXP MCU handles mixed continuous/override commands smoothly.
risk_controls: Keep the object classes very small (e.g., 2 classes).

main_board.name: NXP FRDM-MCXA153
main_board.reasoning: Mandatory board for all summer school projects

sensors.name: Ultrasonic Distance Sensor (e.g., HC-SR04) or IR Distance Sensor
sensors.purpose: Detect physical obstacles for reactive emergency braking.
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: HC-SR04 typically requires 5V logic; use a 3.3V version (HC-SR04+) or level shifting.

sensors.name: IR Line Tracking Sensors
sensors.purpose: Detect lane lines if the camera is not used in the core version.

actuators_outputs.name: DC Motors with H-Bridge Driver (e.g., L298N, TB6612FNG)
actuators_outputs.purpose: Drive the rover and steer via differential drive or a steering servo.
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Requires separate power supply for motors. Ground must be shared with MCU.
risks: High current draw browning out the MCU.

user_inputs.name: Start/Stop Button
user_inputs.purpose: Safely enable or disable the rover.

display_ui.name: Status LEDs
display_ui.purpose: Indicate operating mode (e.g., running, obstacle detected, stop sign).
display_ui.notes: Onboard LEDs of the FRDM-MCXA153 can be used.

communication_debug.name: UART Interface
communication_debug.purpose: Communication link between ESP32-S3 and NXP FRDM-MCXA153.
communication_debug.notes: Requires matched baud rate and crossed RX/TX connections. Both use 3.3V logic.

power_source.notes: Needs step-down converters or buck modules to provide clean 5V/3.3V for MCUs and sensors, while supplying raw battery voltage to motor drivers.

optional_advanced_components.name: ESP32-S3 CAM (OV3660)
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Enables computer vision and TinyML features.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Adds significant software complexity and requires a separate toolchain.
risks: Power hungry when using Wi-Fi or high-fps camera.
Requires custom firmware integration alongside the NXP MCU.

software_context.recommended_development_environment: MCUXpresso IDE or VS Code with NXP extension for FRDM-MCXA153; ESP-IDF or Arduino IDE for ESP32.
recommended_sdk_or_libraries: MCUXpresso SDK (bare-metal drivers for UART, PWM, ADC)
software_context.suggested_starting_point: Hello World and PWM driver examples from MCUXpresso SDK.
possible_gen_ai_usage: code generation for UART parsing and motor mixing

constraints.voltage: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise
constraints.power: Must manage distinct logic and motor power rails securely.
constraints.timing: NXP MCU obstacle avoidance loop must have minimal latency (<50ms).
constraints.memory: NXP MCU memory is sufficient; ESP32 uses PSRAM for image buffering.
constraints.safety: Rover must not exceed safe speeds and must default to STOP on communication loss.
constraints.privacy_security: Local processing only, no cloud streaming of camera feeds required.

complexity.reason: The distributed architecture isolates complex AI tasks (ESP32) from safety-critical real-time control (NXP), making it highly modular and extensible for students.

facts_provided_by_user: ESP32-S3 CAM board handles vision and AI tasks.
NXP FRDM-MCXA153 handles motor PWM and steering.
Ultrasonic/IR sensors connect directly to NXP board.
ESP32 sends UART commands to NXP.
Core 0 of ESP32 does PID lane keeping at 20-30 FPS.
Core 1 of ESP32 does TinyML sign recognition at 3-5 FPS.

assumptions.assumption: The motorized rover platform has differential drive or a servo-steered Ackermann mechanism.
assumptions.reason: Required to convert steering/speed commands into physical motion.

assumptions.assumption: Level shifting is not required for the ESP32 to NXP UART connection.
assumptions.reason: Both ESP32 and MCXA153 typically operate on 3.3V logic.

open_questions.question: What is the exact motor driver IC used?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Determines PWM frequency limits, required logic pins, and current capabilities.

open_questions.question: Will a 3.3V compatible ultrasonic sensor (HC-SR04+) be provided, or standard 5V?
open_questions.why_it_matters: A 5V sensor requires a voltage divider or level shifter on the Echo pin to protect the NXP MCU.

technical: UART message corruption causing erratic movement.
Camera framing and lighting issues causing poor line extraction.
safety: Rover running off table or hitting objects if obstacle avoidance fails.
voltage_power: Brownouts on ESP32 or NXP MCU due to motor current draw.
timing: ESP32 missing frames if Core 1 TinyML tasks starve Core 0.
memory: Running out of internal SRAM on ESP32 if PSRAM is misconfigured.
advanced_feature_risks: Training an accurate TinyML model can be highly time-consuming.

human_approval_required: Battery chemistry and capacity choices for safe lab use.
Approval of motor driver module selection.

handoff_to_requirements_agent.readiness_notes: The conceptual architecture is solid, but exact motor drivers and sensor part numbers must be finalized before circuit design.
critical_missing_information: Exact chassis motor configuration (differential vs. Ackermann).
